It looks like we can get nearly the full benefit of the no-iostream reader implementations that used above but in a fully generalized manner. The reader/writer/flippers accept an IStream/OStream/IOStream template argument. This isn't required to derive from the std iostream interface, just to implement a subset of it. By implementing the simple subset used by reader and writer, this can be passed into any of the byte or byte reader/writer/flipper implementations and based on a comparison of my ad-hoc reader/writer that cut confirmation time by around 55%, it should be very similar.

This supports store serialization, network serialization, header/tx identity hashing, and consensus serialization for signature hashing. Basically everywhere we stream in/out of a fixed buffer. We could also implement a variation for dynamic buffering, but there isn't presently call for it. It looks to be about 1 days work to implement IStream/OStream and one that inherits both (IOStream),  including tests.

Applying these in the various scenarios is then trivial work, just swapping stream types.

elements.text: I did some performance analysis against store reading, which basically amounts to reading txs. This was improved slightly by the new reader, but the bulk of work is in the input/witness/output and these three components are still using the std::iostream reader because (only) these using the chain object serialization. The tools showed that the bulk of time was spent in these specific areas. This is to be expected, as this is the bulk of the store data - but this should then results in comparable improvement in both download/store and read (for validation).

elements.text: Note the obvious inflection points, where the slope increases dramatically. This is the point at which memory becomes filled (256GB) and inefficient paging results. The following points where the slope returns is a restart of the run - in the blue and gray cases. I don't think I restarted it in the orange case. In the orange case I believe the OS dumped about half of the memory, which resolved the issue until it occurred a second time.

elements.text: What's interesting is that performance returns almost immediately after a restart. In other words, performance is only marginally dependent upon the memory cache. The caching of pages is actually hurting performance in the case where a limit is hit, vs. no caching at all.

elements.text: But as for the effectiveness of the stream optimization on reads, a projection (i.e. not memory bound) of the gray run completes at 3.75 hours whereas the blue run projects to 5.83 hours. elements.text: Ok, ran some tests and determined that the difference with the early blocks is entirely caching. The OS caches memory map between runs, and I don't yet have a reliable way to clear the cache. With previously-cached tables the performance is consistent across the block range. The preceding scenarios had both been run with caching in the early stages. In the later stages (fuller blocks) the relative benefit is practically eliminate.

elements.text: Completed the integration of the simple iostream with all network serialization/deserialization and also header/tx hash and signature hash computations. Hard to get a good measure of benefit without a consistent/baseline peer, but the performance analyzer is now showing a pattern I haven't seen before. With validation disabled there are no actual hotspots, tiny values all over. And with validation enabled all hotspots are in libsecp256k1 (signature validation) and a much more modest level in signature hashing and script execution generally. This is what we should expect to see under ideal circumstances.

elements.text: So we're getting to the point where it's time to move on from store optimization and evaluation and get back to networking, with store integration. This would start with implementation of the parallel block downloader with optimized peer selection. The initial target would be to download and store the entire chain in less than one hour on a 1Gbit connection (though I typically see closer to 900Gbit up/down).

elements.text: But first I'm going to take a little detour into a script serialization optimization. Planning to replace the use of
shared_ptr
op-data with
unique_ptr
. These were originally created under the assumption that
shared_ptr
would be the basis of script evaluation, but the generalization to
external_ptr
made that unnecessary.
unique_ptr
eliminates one word per op-data instance and eliminates mutex locks internal to
shared_ptr
. And since a large percentage of these are
nullptr
and scripts are the bulk of the chain, this should be a material optimization, and simple.

text: But first I'm going to take a little detour into a script serialization optimization. Planning to replace the use of `shared_ptr` op-data with `unique_ptr`. These were originally created under the assumption that `shared_ptr` would be the basis of script evaluation, but the generalization to `external_ptr` made that unnecessary. `unique_ptr` eliminates one word per op-data instance and eliminates mutex locks internal to `shared_ptr`. And since a large percentage of these are `nullptr` and scripts are the bulk of the chain, this should be a material optimization, and simple.

elements.text: Overall the store work has come out exceptionally well. system, store, network, and node have proven exceedingly reliable - in fact I'd even dare to say perfectly reliable. In the store work the main issues I had to work through were performance optimization around table structure and some regressions in chain validation due to the full rewrite. The only significant issue, which should not be understated, is thrashing of the memory maps when memory becomes full during significant reading.
